entities.name: Publius Cornelius Lentulus Sura
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Publius Cornelius Lentulus Sura, a scion of the ancient Cornelian gens, served as a prominent Roman senator, achieving the consulship in 71 BCE and the praetorship for a second time in 63 BCE. His historical significance is indelibly tied to his pivotal, albeit disastrous, role as one of the chief conspirators alongside Lucius Sergius Catilina in the plot to overthrow the Roman Republic in 63 BCE. As a former consul, his involvement lent a dangerous legitimacy to the conspiracy, threatening the very fabric of Roman governance and society.

Following his praetorship, Lentulus Sura, burdened by debt and political setbacks, became a key figure in Catiline's second, more desperate attempt to seize power. His specific charge was to organize an uprising within Rome, recruiting disaffected citizens and, critically, attempting to incite a slave revolt and secure military support from the Allobroges, a Gallic tribe. These negotiations with the Allobroges proved to be the undoing of the conspiracy, as the Gauls, seeking better terms from the Senate, betrayed Lentulus Sura and provided incriminating letters to the consul Cicero, leading to the conspirators' swift arrest.

The discovery of his treason and the subsequent senatorial debate culminated in his execution by strangulation in the Tullianum prison on December 5, 63 BCE, alongside other prominent conspirators. This act, carried out without a formal trial before the people, sparked a profound constitutional crisis regarding the Senate's authority to execute Roman citizens, a controversy that would haunt Cicero's political career and contribute to the legal and political instability of the late Republic, ultimately feeding into the civil wars that followed.
